title: T.R. in the Badlands
subtitle: Dakota Territory, 1883–1887
intro: Theodore Roosevelt arrived in Dakota Territory a grieving, asthmatic New York politician who weighed about 135 pounds. He left three years later a working cattleman who could ride from dawn to dusk. Fifteen questions on the country that made him — and on what he did while he was here.
heroAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in fringed buckskin with a rifle, 1885

questions.prompt: What drew Theodore Roosevelt to Dakota Territory in September 1883?
options: He wanted to hunt buffalo before the last herds disappeared
He was sent west on New York State Assembly business
His family owned land in the Badlands
He was recovering from an injury on doctor's orders
questions.explanation: Roosevelt was twenty-four, serving his third Assembly term, and worn thin by the session. He came to shoot a buffalo before there were none left to shoot — and very nearly left it too late. Commercial hunters had destroyed the last great herd along the Little Missouri only months earlier, and he had to hunt for days to find a single bull.
questions.imageAlt: Medora, Dakota Territory, in 1883 — the office and company store of the Marquis de Mores
questions.credit: Medora in 1883 — the office and company store of the Marquis de Mores. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did the men around the Little Missouri call Roosevelt when he first stepped off the train?
options: The Cattle King
The four-eyed dude
Mr. Assemblyman
Old Four Eyes
questions.explanation: He was thin, wore thick spectacles, and dressed like Manhattan. "Dude" meant an Easterner playing at the frontier, and it was not affectionate. Roosevelt does not name the nickname in his Autobiography; it reaches us through the recollections of men who were there, collected decades later.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in his first buckskin suit
questions.credit: "Theodore Roosevelt in his first buckskins." Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who guided Roosevelt on that first buffalo hunt?
options: Bill Sewall
The Marquis de Mores
Joe Ferris
"Hell-Roaring" Bill Jones
questions.explanation: Joe Ferris was barn superintendent at the Pyramid Park Hotel and took the job for a hundred dollars, expecting the Easterner to quit. Instead he watched him fall off horses, get soaked, get lost, and keep going without complaint. Ferris's admiration for the young man's persistence is the thread running through every account of that fortnight.
questions.imageAlt: The store of Joe Ferris at Medora, North Dakota, with a group of men outside
questions.credit: The store of Joe Ferris at Medora, N.D. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did Roosevelt react when he finally killed his first buffalo?
options: He recorded the weight in his hunting journal and moved on
He whooped, danced around the carcass, and beat it with his hat
He refused to take the head as a trophy
He said nothing at all for the rest of the day
questions.explanation: After days of cold rain and sleet, the moment broke him wide open. Joe Ferris, recalling it for Roosevelt's biographer decades later, described him whooping and dancing round the carcass and striking it with his hat — behaviour Ferris had not seen from a grown man before.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in fringed buckskin holding a rifle, 1885
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in 1885. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Before he went home that autumn, Roosevelt wrote a check for $14,000. What did it buy?
options: A half interest in the town of Medora
The Elkhorn Ranch
A stake in the Maltese Cross Ranch
Shares in the Northern Pacific Railroad
questions.explanation: He handed $14,000 to Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield and bought into the Maltese Cross — known equally as the Chimney Butte Ranch — south of Medora, with a starting herd of roughly 450 head. Roosevelt was tickled by the brand. In his Autobiography he noted that "the general impression along the Little Missouri was that 'maltese' must be a plural."
questions.imageAlt: The Maltese Cross Ranch house as it was when Roosevelt lived there
questions.credit: Maltese Cross Ranch house as it was when T.R. lived there. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: On February 14, 1884, Roosevelt suffered a loss that sent him back west for good. What happened?
options: His wife and his mother died in the same house on the same day
His ranch partners dissolved the Maltese Cross agreement
He lost his Assembly seat in a recount
His Manhattan home burned
questions.explanation: His mother, Martha "Mittie" Roosevelt, died of typhoid fever at three in the morning. His wife, Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt, died of Bright's disease that afternoon, two days after giving birth to their daughter. In his diary Roosevelt drew a heavy X and wrote beneath it: "The light has gone out of my life." He almost never spoke of Alice again.
questions.imageAlt: Alice Hathaway Lee, the first Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt
questions.credit: The first Mrs. Theodore Roosevelt (Alice Hathaway Lee). Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt's second ranch, the Elkhorn, got its name from what?
options: A nearby butte shaped like an antler
The brand used by the previous owner
A pair of interlocked elk antlers found on the site
An elk Roosevelt shot on his first day there
questions.explanation: Two bull elk had locked antlers and died together where the ranch house went up — Roosevelt took the name from them. The Elkhorn sat about 35 miles north of Medora in a bend of the Little Missouri, deliberately remote. He called it his "home ranch." Nothing remains today but the foundation stones.
questions.imageAlt: The Elkhorn Ranch house among cottonwoods on the Little Missouri
questions.credit: Elkhorn Ranch, Roosevelt's property on the Little Missouri. Photograph by Theodore Roosevelt. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: See the Elkhorn cabin recreation at the Library

questions.prompt: Roosevelt brought two men out from Maine to run the Elkhorn. Who were they?
options: Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield
Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow
Gregor and Lincoln Lang
Joe Ferris and Arthur Packard
questions.explanation: Bill Sewall was a Maine guide Roosevelt had hired as a teenager in 1878; Wilmot Dow was Sewall's nephew and, by local reckoning, the better shot of the two. Neither had ever worked cattle. Roosevelt wanted men he trusted more than men who knew the business — and Sewall, who was blunt to the point of rudeness, told him hard truths nobody else would.
questions.imageAlt: Wilmot Dow, Theodore Roosevelt, and Bill Sewall in fur coats at the Elkhorn Ranch
questions.credit: Wilmot Dow, T.R., and Bill Sewall at Elkhorn Ranch. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Who founded the town of Medora and named it for his wife?
options: Gregor Lang
Arthur Packard
Theodore Roosevelt
The Marquis de Mores
questions.explanation: Antoine de Vallombrosa, the Marquis de Mores, was a French aristocrat and cavalry officer born the same year as Roosevelt. He founded Medora on April 1, 1883, naming it for his wife, Medora von Hoffman, and sank a fortune into a slaughterhouse meant to ship dressed beef east in refrigerated cars. The Chicago packers beat him. His abattoir chimney still stands.
questions.imageAlt: The house of the Marquis de Mores above the Little Missouri at Medora
questions.credit: The house of the Marquis de Mores from the eastern bank of the river. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Roosevelt also took an unpaid job keeping order in the Badlands. What was it?
options: Deputy sheriff for the northern end of Billings County
Territorial judge at Dickinson
U.S. Marshal for Dakota Territory
Captain of the Medora militia
questions.explanation: He served as deputy sheriff under "Hell-Roaring" Bill Jones, and once told Jones to his face that he was the nastiest talking man he had ever heard. The arrangement was casual: Jones worked as a hired hand on Roosevelt's ranch when the ranch needed hands, and Roosevelt rode as deputy when the county needed a deputy.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt mounted on horseback in ranch clothes near Medora
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in ranch costume. Photograph by T. W. Ingersoll. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: In a hotel barroom, a drunk with two revolvers announced, "Four eyes is going to treat!" What did Roosevelt do?
options: Bought the drinks and left quietly
Drew his own revolver
Knocked the man out with three punches
Sent for the sheriff
questions.explanation: Roosevelt tried to laugh it off and move away first. When that failed, he wrote in his Autobiography: "As I rose, I struck quick and hard with my right just to one side of the point of his jaw, hitting with my left as I straightened out, and then again with my right." The man's guns went off into the ceiling as he dropped. Roosevelt never names the town; it is traditionally identified as Mingusville, now Wibaux, Montana.
questions.imageAlt: The office of the Bad Lands Cow Boy newspaper in Medora
questions.credit: Office of the Bad Lands Cow Boy. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: In March 1886 three men stole something from the Elkhorn and floated off down the Little Missouri. What did they take?
options: Roosevelt's boat
Roosevelt's saddle horses
The ranch's winter supplies
The Elkhorn cattle brand irons
questions.explanation: They took the scow — the flat-bottomed boat that was the ranch's only crossing of an ice-choked river. Sewall and Dow built a replacement in a few days below freezing, and on March 30 the three men launched it downstream after the thieves. Roosevelt packed Tolstoy's Anna Karenina and a volume of Matthew Arnold to read by the fire.
questions.imageAlt: The Little Missouri River winding through the Badlands
questions.credit: "A plains river" — the Little Missouri. Photograph by Theodore Roosevelt. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: After capturing the thieves, Roosevelt turned down the easy option. What did he do instead?
options: Let them go with a warning
Handed them to local cowboys, who would almost certainly have hanged them
Marched them roughly 100 miles overland to the sheriff at Dickinson
Held them at the ranch until spring
questions.explanation: Hanging was what the country expected, and cowboys were on hand to do it. Roosevelt refused. He kept the three prisoners moving for some 36 hours to Dickinson, walking behind them with a Winchester and reading Matthew Arnold to stay awake. His feet blistered so badly that Dr. Victor Stickney had to treat them; his fee for the job was about fifty dollars. He later called it the most important thing he did in the Badlands — not because it was brave, but because choosing a hundred-mile march over a rope argued that law belongs even where there is no courthouse. (The thieves drew twenty-five months, not the three years some accounts report.)
questions.imageAlt: A staged photograph of Roosevelt guarding the boat thieves on a riverbank
questions.credit: "T.R. guarding the boat thieves" — a re-creation staged after the fact, with Sewall, Dow, and an unidentified man posing as the prisoners. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: The winter of 1886–87 ended the open range. What did ranchers call it, and what did it cost Roosevelt?
options: The Long Freeze — he lost about a quarter of his herd
The Great Die-Up — he lost roughly 60 to 80 percent of his herd
The Blue Winter — he lost his ranch buildings
The Hard Snow — he lost nothing, having sold out in the fall
questions.explanation: Temperatures fell to forty below and stayed. The range had been eaten bare by overstocking, so the cattle went into the storms already starving. Roosevelt came back in the spring of 1887 to find the coulees full of carcasses and the greater part of his herd dead — estimates run from 60 to 80 percent. It ended the open-range cattle boom on the northern plains.
questions.imageAlt: A large herd of cattle on the northern plains
questions.credit: Cattle on the range. Photograph by L. A. Huffman. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

link.label: How the range shaped his conservation

questions.prompt: Looking back, how did Roosevelt weigh his Dakota years against the rest of his life?
options: He called them a pleasant interruption
He credited them with making his presidency possible
He regretted the money he had lost there
He rarely referred to them once he left
questions.explanation: He said more than once that he would never have been president but for his years in North Dakota — a remark that reaches us through those who heard it rather than through anything he wrote, and which survives in slightly different wordings. What is not in doubt is the transformation: he arrived at about 135 pounds with asthma that had shadowed his whole life, and left at about 170 without it.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt standing next to his horse on the roundup, 1885
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt on the round-up, 1885. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
